Definitions

Artificial Intelligence (AI)
: refers to the development or use of computer systems that can perform tasks that typically require human intelligence, such as learning, problem-solving, decision-making, and perception.

Machine Learning (ML):
a subset of AI involving algorithms and statistical models to enable machines to learn from data without being explicitly programmed.

Deep Learning (DL):
a subset of ML that involves the use of neural networks with multiple layers to learn complex patterns in data.

Here is a sample statement provided by Dr. Dean Taciuch, College of Humanities and Social Sciences:

“Generative-AI tools, such as ChatGPT and Microsoft Co Pilot, should not be used in this course unless specified by the assignment. Use of such tools presents ethical and academic dishonesty issues, especially if the work is presented as your own. While such tools may be used to generate ideas, brainstorm, or outline larger works, the language in work you submit in this course should always be your own. Submitted work that is not your own is an Academic Integrity violation (“Providing, using, or attempting to benefit from unauthorized academic material and/or assistance”).

I will not use AI-detection software in this course, as it is unreliable and likely makes the generative AI software even less detectable, as the submitted works become part of the generative AI corpus. If you do use generative AI software, you will be responsible for any incorrect, biased, or unethical information that is submitted.

Finally, you must be transparent with your use even on assignments in which you are permitted to use Generative AI.”

Dean Taciuch, Term Professor, English, College of Humanities and Social Sciences

E.1 Ethical Use Policy
Georgia Southern is committed to ensuring AI tools adopted within, teaching, learning,
research, operations, and administrative support contexts uphold the highest standards of
ethical integrity. AI use must align with the mission. Accordingly, AI tools procured and utilized
by stakeholders must adhere to the following principles and effective safeguards.
● Fairness/Mitigation of Bias: AI tools must be evaluated for potential biases in their
design, training data, and outputs. It should actively demonstrate efforts to reduce bias
and promote equitable outcomes for members of the university community.
● Accountability: Clear lines of accountability are essential. Vendors must provide
transparent documentation of how their tools function, what data they rely on, and how
they are maintained.

● Reliability and Factual Accuracy: Tools will be assessed for reliability and accuracy. AI

undergo additional scrutiny or may be disallowed.
● Human Oversight: AI should support, not replace, human judgment. The vendor must
support functionality to allow users to review outputs generated through AI tools by
providing clear documentation of the tool’s capabilities and limitations.
● Accessibility: AI tools must be accessible to all users, including those with disabilities.
● Risk Mitigation Systems: Systems must be assessed for vulnerabilities, including
susceptibility to prompt injection attacks or malicious manipulation.
AI users must take appropriate steps to protect data and sensitive information when using AI
tools and be aware that feeding data into unsecured public AI models is potentially the same
as posting it in a public location. Only publicly available data may be entered/used in public AI
tools. Data classified as “Confidential” (Class 1) or “Sensitive” (Class 2) according to the Data
Stewardship and Classification Standard should only be provided to AI models that are listed
in the approved inventory of AI tools.
